title: Greetings & First Words
subtitle: Break the ice with locals
description: Hello, thank you, sorry, yes, no. The phrases that make every interaction warmer. Locals genuinely appreciate when you try.

items.context: Universal greeting that works any time of day — more respectful than a casual hi, used by everyone from street vendors to office colleagues
items.scenario: Opening any conversation, from meeting your landlord to greeting your PG owner in the morning

items.context: Use this until around noon — literally 'auspicious morning', a warm and pleasant way to start the day
items.scenario: Greeting your neighbor, office receptionist, or the canteen staff in the morning

items.context: Said from late afternoon onwards — sanje means evening, the golden hour when Bengaluru comes alive
items.scenario: Walking back to your PG, meeting someone at a bus stop, or greeting someone at evening tea

items.context: The formal version — use nīvu (you, formal) with elders, landlords, shopkeepers, and anyone older than you
items.scenario: Asking your PG owner, a professor, or an older colleague how they're doing

items.context: Casual version for friends and peers — nīnu is the friendly you, use it with classmates and flatmates
items.scenario: Texting a Kannada-speaking friend or asking your hostel roommate how they're doing

items.context: The standard reply when asked how you're doing — chenna means beautiful or good, and this is genuinely a warm phrase
items.scenario: Responding to anyone who asks nīvu hēgiddīri? or nīnu hēgiddīya?

items.context: The formal, complete thank-you — dhanya means blessed, vāda means expression. Use this in professional or formal settings
items.scenario: Thanking a shopkeeper who helped you find something, or expressing gratitude to a colleague

items.context: Works both as an apology and to politely get someone's attention — the softest, most useful phrase in your kit
items.scenario: Bumping into someone in a crowd, interrupting to ask a question, or getting an auto driver's attention

items.context: Literally 'nothing needed' — the relaxed, friendly response when someone thanks you or apologises
items.scenario: When a colleague or neighbour thanks you for something small, wave it off with this

items.context: A gentle, natural way to say you're heading out — less abrupt than just walking away
items.scenario: Leaving the office, wrapping up a conversation with your landlord, or heading out from a shop

items.context: A warm parting phrase — matte means again, sigōṇa means let us meet. Locals will smile when they hear this
items.scenario: Parting with someone you expect to see again — your dosa-wala, a friendly neighbour, or a new acquaintance

items.context: Add this at the start of any request to soften it immediately — without it, requests can sound abrupt
items.scenario: Before asking for anything: dayaviṭṭu nīru koḍi (please give me water), dayaviṭṭu illi nilisi (please stop here)

items.context: The standard yes — also used to confirm what someone said, like 'right' or 'that's correct'
items.scenario: Confirming an address with your auto driver, agreeing to a price, or answering any yes/no question

items.context: Not just no — illa also means 'there isn't any' or 'it doesn't exist'. One of the most versatile words you'll use
items.scenario: Refusing when an auto driver tries to overcharge, or when a shop doesn't have what you need

items.context: The everyday go-to for agreement — not as strong as yes, more like 'alright then' or 'got it'
items.scenario: Agreeing to plans, wrapping up instructions from your landlord, or confirming you understand something
